content: In vertebrate anatomy, ribs, known in Latin as costae, are elongated, curved bones that constitute the ribcage. In most animals, ribs encircle the thorax (Latin: thorax) and serve to protect vital thoracic organs such as the lungs, heart, and other internal structures. In certain species, particularly snakes, ribs extend along the body, providing structural support and additional protection. Human Anatomy Humans, regardless of sex, possess 24 ribs, arranged in 12 pairs. The first seven pairs of ribs are directly connected to the sternum via their own individual costal cartilage. These are referred to as true ribs. The remaining five pairs are classified as false ribs. Among these, the first three pairs of false ribs share a common cartilaginous connection to the sternum, while the last two pairs, the eleventh and twelfth ribs, are termed floating ribs (Latin: costae fluitantes) or vertebral ribs. Floating ribs are attached solely to the vertebrae and lack any connection to the sternum or its associated cartilage. It is worth noting that some individuals may naturally lack one of the two pairs of floating ribs, while others may have an additional, third pair. Rib removal, a surgical procedure, involves the excision of ribs for either therapeutic or cosmetic purposes. The ribcage is anatomically separated from the lower abdominal cavity by the thoracic diaphragm, a muscular structure essential for respiration. During contraction of the diaphragm, the ribcage and thoracic cavity expand, reducing intrathoracic pressure and facilitating the influx of air into the lungs. Ribs in Other Animals In mammals, ribs are typically associated with the thoracic region. However, during embryonic development, remnants of ribs can be observed in the cervical vertebrae (cervical ribs) and sacral vertebrae, where they are fused. In reptiles, ribs may be present along the entire vertebral column, extending from the neck to the sacrum. Turtles exhibit a unique adaptation, where their ribs have evolved into a bony or cartilaginous shell, comprising the carapace and plastron. In fish, the number of ribs can vary significantly, with some species, such as herring, displaying up to four ribs per vertebra. However, not all fish possess this many ribs, and the rib structure can differ widely among species.
